old: tore out his genitals and threw them raw to the dogs
new: drew out his vitals and gave them raw to the dogs
reason: Coordinator ruling: Butler writes "they drew out his vitals and gave them to the dogs raw"; "genitals" imports the Greek sense beyond the locked source, so Butler's "vitals" is restored unsoftened (also restores his "drew out"/"gave" for the added "tore"/"threw"); the drafter's note that keeps "genitals" is overruled.

old: hook-beaked, sharp-taloned eagles
new: eagle-beaked, crook-taloned vultures
reason: Butler: "As eagle-beaked, crook-taloned vultures from the mountains swoop down"; the candidate changes the bird to eagles and drops Butler's "eagle-beaked".

old: so she scolded Odysseus angrily. “Odysseus, your strength
new: so she scolded Odysseus very angrily. “Odysseus,” she said, “your strength
reason: Butler: "she scolded Ulysses very angrily. “Ulysses,” said she, “your strength"; the candidate drops the speech tag (the only paragraph whose quotation-mark count differs from Butler's, 1/1 against 2/2) and the intensifier "very", unlike the restored tag structure at 22 and 41.

old: lifting a beautiful golden cup
new: lifting a two-handled gold cup
reason: Butler: "about to take up a two-handled gold cup"; the concrete "two-handled" is dropped and "beautiful" is invented.

old: one of the other men might attack him with a sword or club him down
new: one of the Achaeans might come up and hack at him with a sword or knock him down
reason: Butler: "some one of the Achaeans might come up and hack at him with his sword, or knock him down"; the name is dropped, "hack" is softened to "attack", and "club" invents a weapon.

old: we’d soon end this man’s shooting
new: we’d soon make an end of this man and his shooting
reason: Butler: "we should soon make an end of this man and his shooting"; the candidate ends only the shooting and drops the killing of the man.

old: another’s bronze point hit the wall
new: the pointed shaft of another struck the wall
reason: Butler: "the pointed shaft of another struck the wall"; "bronze" is invented, the same class the drafter removed from the arrow-point at 1.

old: another’s bronze point hit the wall
new: the pointed shaft of another struck the wall
reason: Butler repeats "the pointed shaft of another struck the wall" from 26; "bronze" is invented, and the repetition should match 26.

old: In the end he decided it was best
new: In the end he thought it best
reason: Butler: "in the end he deemed it best"; the fixed GLOSSARY formula ("deemed it best" → "thought it best", accepted B05-P037, B06-P012, B10, B18) is not applied.

old: from the streams of Ocean,
new: from the streams of Oceanus,
reason: Butler: "from the streams of Oceanus"; already-Greek names stay exactly as Butler spells them, and accepted Books 10, 11, 19 and 20 print "Oceanus".

old: slung a four-layered shield over his shoulders
new: slung a shield four hides thick over his shoulders
reason: Butler: "hung a shield four hides thick about his shoulders"; the material (hides) is dropped, and GLOSSARY Voice and form keeps materials exactly.

old: The contest is finished. Now I’ll see if Apollo will grant me the power to hit a target no man has ever struck before.
new: The mighty contest is over. Now I’ll see whether Apollo will grant that I hit another target, one no man has yet hit.
reason: Butler: "The mighty contest is at an end. I will now see whether Apollo will vouchsafe it to me to hit another mark which no man has yet hit"; "mighty" and the pointed "another" (the next mark is Antinous) are dropped and "the power" is added.

old: become the ruler of Ithaca
new: become chief man in Ithaca
reason: Butler: "to be chief man in Ithaca"; "ruler" is a stronger claim, and "chief" is a word the edition holds steady (GLOSSARY chief vs master).

old: And we should spare Medon too
new: And we will spare Medon too
reason: Butler: "and we will spare Medon too"; "should" turns Telemachus's statement into a suggestion.

old: The man is innocent—don’t harm him!
new: The man is innocent. Don’t harm him!
reason: Butler: "the man is guiltless, do him no hurt"; a comma, so the added dash breaks the Book 10 lesson (no dash where Butler has a comma).

old: But I know what I’ll do—I’ll bring you weapons
new: But I know what I’ll do. I’ll bring you weapons
reason: Butler: "But I know what I will do, I will bring you arms"; the dash is added where Butler has a comma, and a sentence break is enough.

old: Tell me—should I kill him
new: Tell me, should I kill him
reason: Butler: "Say, shall I kill him"; the dash is added where Butler has a comma.

old: in the other—one that Laertes had carried
new: in the other, one that Laertes had carried
reason: Butler: "an old dry-rotted shield in the other, which had been borne by Laertes"; the dash is added where Butler has a comma.

old: and kill them—for they cannot fight or fly
new: and kill them, for they cannot fight or fly
reason: Butler: "and kill them, for they cannot either fight or fly"; the first dash is added where Butler has a comma (his one dash, before "even so", is kept).

old: as their skulls were crushed, and the ground ran red with blood
new: as their brains were battered in, and the ground seethed with their blood
reason: Butler: "as their brains were being battered in, and the ground seethed with their blood"; the gore and the seething image are both changed.

old: dangerously close to the courtyard door
new: dangerously close to the entrance to the outer court
reason: Butler: "dangerously near the entrance to the outer court"; the outer court is a fixed place in this Book (33, 37, 38), and "courtyard door" blurs it.

old: Can’t someone go to the trap door
new: Can’t someone go up to the trap door
reason: Butler: "Cannot some one go up to the trap door"; "up" tells the listener where the trap door is.

old: Then tie a rope around his body
new: Then fasten a noose around his body
reason: Butler: "then fasten a noose about his body"; "rope" generalizes the concrete noun.

old: Then they fastened a rope around his body
new: Then they fastened a noose around his body
reason: Butler: "then they fastened a noose about his body", repeating 19's order; "rope" generalizes it.

old: its straps now loose and frayed
new: its straps now come unstitched
reason: Butler: "the straps had become unsewn"; "frayed" is invented.

old: and bring weapons for the swineherd
new: and bring armor for the swineherd
reason: Butler: "will bring other armour for the swineherd and the stockman"; armor, not weapons.

old: my child,” Eurycleia answered
new: my son,” Eurycleia answered
reason: Butler: "I will tell you the truth, my son,"; the address is changed.

old: you’re so pathetically weak now
new: you’re so lamentably less valiant now
reason: Butler: "so lamentably less valiant now"; the comparative with the former Odysseus becomes an absolute insult.

old: looked around desperately for somewhere to escape
new: looked around for somewhere to escape
reason: Butler: "every man looked round about to see whither he might fly for safety"; "desperately" is an added intensifier.

old: We have done terrible wrongs
new: We have done much wrong
reason: Butler: "We have done much wrong"; "terrible" intensifies it.

old: He toppled backward
new: He toppled over
reason: Butler: "he fell over"; "backward" invents a direction.

old: Everything you’ve said is right
new: Everything you’ve said is true
reason: Butler: "All that you have said is true".
